Tyler thought he was doing a hangdog job of hiding his disappointment. Instead, as he made his way off the stage, he began dragging his feet and acting like a child. He kept thinking that the reason for his blocks in life, his constant second-place jobs and slow processing speed, was that he just couldn't keep a steady focus. He'd been focused for months, but still came in second; obviously, he still wasn't trying hard enough.

He let his backpack drop to the floor in his empty, tiny apartment. He pulled a full bottle of clarety from the back of the cupboard and poured himself a drink. He wasn't sure he could face cooking again for a while, but he still bought groceries: six whole-grain loaves, a bag of nectarines, new pots and spatulas. One by one, he threw them in the trash.

Tyler answered his door in the evening. Evelyn stood there, holding the white box in front of her.

"I think this belongs to you," she said. She hadn't been the one to drop the box on stage after all. "I found it when I was packing up my entries." She paused and said brightly, "I think one of our pies is missing."

Tyler laughed, then heberated himself in his head and offered Evelyn a drink. Evelyn thought his laugh sounded forced. She shifted the box from one hand to the other and laughed too, but with more warmth. She wanted Tyler to feel better, but didn't know what to say. Then something popped into her head. She said, "I lost a fair too, once. I have a photograph of it. Would you like to see?"

Evelyn Parrish shakily put her hand on Tyler's shoulder. Later she'd say that he had evil news coming for him and that she couldn't bear to see a boy's heart break. But that afternoon, she smiled at Tyler, her lips quivering, eyes glistening, and it looked like she might cry.

Tyler knew what other people thought about Evelyn Parrish: she was depressed that she'd lost this year, she was a kind old lady at war with herself over the secret she'd uncovered, she was on opioids for an aching hip. But Evelyn gravitated toward him like a parent with a lonely child. She taught him how to make a three-layer lattice crust and revealed a foolproof pie crust method that she refined over decades in the back room of Hollister's Bakery. On family visits home from college, he stayed with Evelyn and helped her in the garden.

At life's end she bequeathed her home to him: a one-story farmhouse from 1862, with four rooms, an uneven foundation, gingerbread trim, and a fire that would've leveled the place if it hadn't been discovered on a Saturday afternoon when she was at the mall, picking up jars of fruit-infused honey. Over the next year, he paid off the Federal Hold taught her in his software engineering classes.

"At the end of the day, I am still a regular person." Tyler prefers to say "I hack," though without the implied criminality the word carries now.

A Cybersecurity Solutions Engineer is like a lock picker. He anticipates a company's possible vulnerabilities, penetrates their firewall, and creates countermeasures to prevent an actual attack. In this the second year of his career, his specialty was Ethernet jammers, devices the size of solid-state hard drives that can "sniff out" a wifi signal and interfere with the way data travels through it. On a weekday afternoon you'll find him at his home office, an almost windowless room tucked between the garage (where he keeps Evelyn's hand-built cherry pies) and his bedroom, behind a stack of logistics textbooks. A river of broadband data is on one screen, the map appears on the other. Every commentary, every best-in-show, every tribute post is from before his childhood, as if he were a person who arrived on Earth full-formed, age sixten, after the last fire.

Since he didn't understand why his father had to go to California, Devon basked in being an only child. He used Tyler's toothbrush and was bored three seconds after Tyler left with a look that said how awful having two dads could be.

On his thirteenth birthday, Garrett Hecht asked for a chimney sweep. His parents got him a set of plastic swords and a padded helmet, with the dragon sticker still on it. But the burning question had to do with the Lair, a velvet-covered alcove in the basement with gilt brocade curtains—it was definitely a room, and it would have made a good kitchen.

Garrett was brave. Once, after getting a bad haircut, he showed up at an assembly at Victor Grove Elementary wearing a cone-shaped hat and sparklers. He needed a chimney sweep and, not having any house elves, he found Candy Bacon. At the beginning of that school year, Candy smelled garlic and onions most of the time, and she spent her free period making plans: homework, football practice, driver's ed., workout, laundry, air mattress, whatever. Although if you were lucky and asked her to stay the day of a game, she would give you her set of Duane Troxel posters. That October, when Garrett looked over his shoulder and asked her if she wanted to be a chimney sweep, and wore a cape and a princely hat, and stayed in the Lair all night, and talked about swords, she said yes. There didn't seem to be much of a risk involved. But then they fell asleep, and at three in the morning Garrett woke up and Candy was gone.

She went home and stayed in a closet, the closet at the top of the stairs in the house with trapdoors in the floors, that had a row of the rubber horse heads her mom had collected growing up. She was ashamed, because she had let herself in, even when Garrett told her the room was for princes and she called him a con and kept turning the doorknob. Some princes didn't take no for an answer. "A hunter was once traveling through the jungle when he found an egg bigger than his head. It was as white as snow and as round as a baseball. He picked it up and carried it back to his village. For forty years, the egg was displayed in the village square. Every day, thousands of people came from all over to look at this egg. But no one believed it was real. On the fortieth anniversary of the egg’s discovery, a man on the edge of the crowd called out, ‘I bet this isn’t even a chicken egg.’ His pitiless rebuke provoked cheers. ‘If it’s a chicken egg,’ he said, ‘let it hatch.’ He took the egg from the pedestal and handed it to the hunter who had found it. ‘Here,’ he said. ‘You start. Booklist Review

Tragedy begets tragedy in Ryan's (Esperanza Rising) tale of a Depression-era family's strife. Tyler is a blues lover with a knack for baking. He works as a short-order cook and dreams of attending a seven-week summer program in the bakery arts at the Rockingham Institute of Household Training to gain entrance to the Culinary Institute in New Orleans. A nasty prank forces the Pie Prince to abandon his fantasy. His grieving and extravagantly nurturing mother resents the rupture and wants her offered first-place prize. Eventually, after several thwarted schemes and much internal anguish, Tyler forgives and finds his mother. The surrounding cast, including his inherently good but feckless father and the rejected but courageous Evelyn, are all solidly imagined. Although some readers will have experience with this period in history, Ryan nevertheless offers a fresh and relevant voice in her take on the struggles and triumphs of Depression America. The central psychological issues of holding on (Tyler's mother) and letting go (Tyler) have legitimate universal application. ?Delias Winnnegram, Antioch University New England, NH Copyright 2014 Booklist

...Harlow's Bakery in Harlow, Kansas." She handed the ribbon to Evelyn.

Tyler tried not to look surprised, but he had rehearsed disappointment all summer and felt almost ready for it. Evelyn put her arms around him and patted his back like she was his grandmother. Margaret left right after the awards were handed out. Evelyn swabbed cherry filling from the edge of her pie and silently passed her linen napkin to Tyler. Tyler had brought two. He wiped his hands and then carefully wiped down her pie, removing all traces of filling from the pristine white aluminum pan.

"Thank you," Evelyn said. She had a very steady voice, more steady than his.

"One time my mom entered a cupcake with a rolled fondant to look like a steering wheel. It came in last. But the judges said it was the most creative thing they'd ever tasted."

"They did?"

"Yeah."

"It's nice to be first sometimes, but it's good to be remembered, too."

Tyler nodded. He put the napkin in his pocket.

He took the ribbon out of the box at home. It smelled like cherry filling. He typed an e-mail to the summer cooking program with the details for booking and asked his mother if she could take out a cash advance on her credit card.

The summer before, Tyler had burned the hair off the back of his left hand while using a kitchen torch too close to a pot of crème brûlée. His mother had taken a photo of the red, swollen flesh with her cell phone. His father had printed it out, and it hung on the refrigerator, right between the magnets and the tabletop calendar with the kittens wearing aprons. Tyler's hand had healed by next week, but the picture stayed up for the rest of the summer. Everyone who came over eat pie looked at it and said things like "Be careful, or you'll get fingers instead of thumbs."

Now Tyler placed the blue ribbon beside the photo. It looked strange and out of place, but not as strange as the burn.

The whole rest of the day after that, rain or no rain, Tyler sampled everything at the fair: candy-apple popsicles, fried Oreos, mini donuts glazed so hard they'd stick to your teeth. He ate funnel cake and broiled corn. That night he split a caramel apple with his little sister, Marlee. Neither of them said anything about the ribbon.

But a few days later, Tyler started making his list for next year's pie. He bought new pencils and a spiral-bound notebook, logged on to epicurious.com, wrote an e-mail to the Kickstarter people who'd responded to his summer-program proposal. In late September, he read an article about food-safety violations at the Delmar County Fair: mouse droppings behind the barbecue tent, undercooked sausage, raw chicken left out in the sun. They'd given the county government two months to clean up its act or risk losing the contract for next year's fair. As he read the article, Tyler remembered the white box from Hollister's Bakery—he thought he recognized the bakery's logo from a TV commercial. He remembered how it had slipped halfway out of Evelyn's bag. He pictured Margaret Lund reading the label: "Moon Pie, Made in Tennessee." Then he remembered how Evelyn had defended her spot in line, how she'd flinched when Margaret had looked at her, how she'd pushed the box back into her bag.

The next morning, he woke his parents before they were scheduled to leave for work. "Can we talk about the fair?" he asked.

His mom set her coffee on the dining-room table and nodded.

Tyler said, "I think Evelyn cheated."

His mom and dad exchanged a look.

"I'm serious," he said. "I bet that was her pie. That box had the logo on it."

His mom said, "You can't really know that."

"I want to tell someone," Tyler said. "I want them to look into it."

His dad picked at a crack in the tabletop. "The pie competition is important for the county fair. It brings in people." He looked at his wife, who shrugged. He kept looking at Tyler. "There's nothing we can do," he said.

"Maybe I won't enter," he said, even though he already knew he would.

Later, though, he took the cash prize down to the checkout stand to buy the summer cooking program. The girl there had purple hair, three piercings, and a tattoo of a fox's head on her left wrist. She wore the same red-polka-dot uniform as every other worker in the building, but the tattoo gave her away as someone who wanted to be noticed.

She rang up the cooking program, then looked through the tiny glass window at the shelf behind her, as if she might change her mind and decide to give him something for free. She looked at Tyler's shoes, at his face, then back at the register screen, and finally she cleared her throat and said, "Congratulations."

"Thanks," he said, and wondered why she sounded so surprised. He further wondered why she sounded like she might be the one who needed to be congratulated.

He took his bag and headed for the door. Outside he opened the sack and breathed deep: it smelled like honest work, like ambition, and like a future.

. . . Tyler Nguyen."

Evelyn clapped loudly, as did Tyler's parents. Tyler's brother gave a whoop.

When Tyler stepped forward to accept the ribbon, he saw that Margaret was holding something else, something plain and small in her other hand. She smiled at Evelyn and offered it to her. It was the plastic medallion she always awarded for second place. Evelyn took it without looking at it, but when she got it in her hand she looked at Margaret. Margaret nodded. Evelyn looked down at the medallion, turned it in her fingers, and for a long time didn't say anything.

Finally she said, "Thank you," like she meant it, loud enough for everyone to hear.

Later, as Tyler was leaving the fairgrounds, Evelyn approached his family at the car.

"I just want to say," she told him, "congratulations. That pie was lovely." Then she leaned down to him and whispered, "That crust was a miracle."

And Tyler thought that if she was going to whisper, she must really mean it. He thanked her and said he was glad she liked it.

"You know what my problem was?" Evelyn said, but without waiting for an answer held out her hand, and in it was the plastic second-place medallion. "This?"

He nodded, and she continued. "This is the first one I've ever gotten. My husband used to do the crust."

She backed away from them a little and set a palm to her chest. "I'm going to learn. Next year you won't get my cherry pie," she said, then turned away and disappeared into the August dusk.

In the car Tyler decided not to tell his parents about the medallion and its secret. He put the blue ribbon on the rearview mirror. It fluttered a little as they drove away from the fair, but when he touched it, it grew still, and as they followed the highway into the countryside, the ribbon stayed there, gleaming, as steady as a small piece of sky.

Tyler stood up and smiled as Margaret put the ribbon on his pie and handed him the check. Then Margaret lifted Evelyn's pie and set it on the runner-up table.

"I thought I'd give it a try," Tyler said later. The county fair was winding down and the tent was empty. His parents were waiting near the pickup. He was counting the ribbon money and putting it in his pocket. He worried Evelyn Parrish might demand it back.

She walked over from the bake tent, a small box tucked under her arm. Tyler thought she looked old and tired. She nodded at Margaret, who had come to search for her car keys in the weeds.

"Congratulations," Evelyn said to Tyler. "That was a good pie."

"Thank you."

She paused, looking at the ribbon in his hand.

"Maybe next year, you could share first place," she said. Then she handed him the box without looking at him and walked away.

Inside the box was a pie, still warm. Tyler couldn't remember the last time he'd been given a pie. His mother had brought him a slice of his own for luck that morning. This was a double-crust blueberry with a latticework top that gleamed like something precious. Tyler didn't know what to do with it. Evelyn hadn't said anything else. He tilted the box. A perfect blueberry rolled out onto his shoe. He picked it up and put it in his pocket, along with the ribbon money and the feeling that he should have done something else.

. . ." There was a pause. The crowd waited. Margaret looked around at all the contestants. Tyler's stomach plummeted. Had he done something wrong? Was his crust flaky enough? Had he seasoned the apples just right?

"Evelyn Parrish," Margaret said finally.

A small cheer went up. Eleanor Wilcox, who was Evelyn's neighbor, hugged her. Evelyn looked surprised and a little dazed.

The second place was Margo Hines's dutch apple, and third place went to Tyler.

Margaret Lund found Tyler at the table where he and his parents were cutting the remaining slice of pie. She handed him a wide, navy-blue ribbon and touched his shoulder. Her fingernails were blue, too, from some kind of polish that looked like dried ink.

"Congratulations," Margaret said. "The ribbon's a little early, I know." She smiled and nodded at the tent where Evelyn was cutting a piece of her winning pie. "But I had to talk to Evelyn before I gave it to you. You'd have done the same thing if you'd been in her place. I hope you understand."

Tyler nodded, but didn't know what to say.

"I have good news for you," Margaret said. "You got into the cooking institute." Her eyes twinkled. "And Evelyn helped with it."

Tyler didn't know what to think. His chest felt airy and light, as if he'd run up three flights of stairs and was just standing there to catch his breath.

She patted his shoulder again. "Don't let anyone tell you it's not right to bake for your own glory. But don't ever let that be the only reason you bake. And never forget to be nice, too. All right?"

Tyler nodded again, and when he looked up, Margaret was walking away. She didn't go back to the judging table, but into the green shade behind the animal exhibits. She was a small, bent-over woman, and she was alone.

A group of teenagers from Harlow High School clustered by the door, homecoming-rianne Hawaiian shirts and jeadow-aram bush hats. One of them, a blonde boy who was one of Tyler's neighbors, had a talent for accents. He looked at Tyler and said in a very passable British accent, "Tough break, mate."

Margaret hurried over and gave the blue ribbon to the other pie. "I meant to say this goes to Tyler Nguyen." She handed it to him and waved at the crowd to start applauding. Many people clapped, but some looked confused, or at Evelyn, who was still clutching her recipe box.

Evelyn raised her eyebrows at Margaret. "Did you make a mistake, Margaret?"

Margaret opened her mouth, then shut it, and then looked at the ground. "No," she said softly. "I didn't make a mistake. I can tell the difference between a cherry pie and an apple pie."

Evelyn didn't say anything.

The British-accent boy looked at his friends and said, in his regular voice, "I guess he wins." Tyler left the tent, ribbon clutched in one hand, apples in the other.

Later, when Tyler got home, he broke his rule about slicing into pie crusts and ate a big wedge of the first-place pie. He couldn't taste the difference, either.

You're going to Kansas City," Evelyn said.

"Thank you," Tyler said.

"You'll have an amazing time," she said, her voice cracking. "But if you see any of my pies there, don't let them copy my lattice top. That's a Parrish family secret." She laughed and dabbed at her eyes, and for a moment Tyler wondered if she was going to cry. Then she handed him a card from her purse and pressed it into his hand, along with the blue ribbon.

"Write to me if you enter the contest again," she said. "Tell me what you learn in Kansas City."

"I will," Tyler said.

After Evelyn left the tent, Margaret Lund walked back over to the baking table and picked up the pie Tyler had entered and the one the judges had just scored behind her. She returned with a small knife and cut out a piece of each pie, then set both pieces on a paper plate.

"Try them side by side," Margaret said. "Tell me what you notice."

Tyler set the two pieces next to each other on the edge of the table and ate.

Evelyn's crust was thick, and where she'd put the slit for the filling to vent, she had poked the dough so hard that it had pinched in. Tyler's was even, the vent cut with a knife. Both had enough sugar to make the tartness of the cherries pop, but Evelyn's had more brown sugar, and her filling had a heavier, molasses note under the sweet.

His tasted brighter. Evelyn's was better in some ways, but he liked his better.

"I'd agree with the decision," Margaret said.

Tyler nodded, then looked back at the plate, at the two pieces of pie next to each other.

A minute later Margaret came out and walked over to him. He thought she was going to tell him he'd done something wrong. Instead she sat down at the table and gestured for him to move his plate.

She didn't say anything for a full minute. Then she said, "You have the recipe for that pie written down?"

"Most of it."

"Could I have a copy?"

"Sure." Tyler kept looking at his hands.

Margaret waited while he found his notebook and copied out his recipe. She pinned the sheet to the top of her clipboard.

She said, "You have talent. The rich flavor of your apples, the hint of lemon zest—it was great baking. But the secret to the best pies is in the crust. You need to keep working on it. Next time, make more of it, and make it flakier."

Tyler took a bite of pie. He looked at her.

She went on, "The one thing everyone remembers from their first pie contest is the experience. I remember my first contest. I was seven, and my apple cheese got me third place. But they gave me a blue sticker, and I thought it was the prettiest thing I'd ever seen. I baked pies for the next forty-nine years because of that sticker."

She tapped his pie with her fork, just once. "That pie is beautiful. You ought to be proud of it."

She left. Tyler wasn't sure if he was proud. He wasn't sure what he was. He finished his pie.

After the visitors had gone and the exhibits were being put away, Margaret found a piece of chalk and walked over to Evelyn's display. She wrote, in careful letters, "Congratulations on #12." Then she put a blue sticker just under the ribbon on Tyler's pie box.

After the awards, he went back for his blue ribbon and talked to a few friends from school, and then to Margaret. "Can I take you to coffee?" he asked. Until he was fifteen, Tyler swore he was straight. Then he took a picture from the yearbook to his room, tried to fashion board shorts out of a sheet, wondered how long it would be before he would want his dad to stop calling his boyfriends "girlfriend." In short: he was in trouble.

Margaret had had a lot of boyfriends. She didn't know what she would do with a boyfriend now, seventy-three and mostly retired from her farm office, but Tyler needed somebody to go to coffee with who understood boyfriends.

Rain kept falling through the night, until a few hours before dawn, when it started to lighten up. Tyler woke up and watched it rain: the small, high-pitched sound of fat drops hitting the windowsills in his bedroom. He thought about all the pies that had gone into his blue ribbon — how he'd spent the summer mixing margarine until the streaks were gone, pulsing twelve times to the beat of a song, and then twelve more; keeping pastry dry; how he'd agonized over the cherries, the juice, the egg wash, the lattice pattern. There were worse single-minded purposes than four months on pies.

The rain was the sound he'd been falling asleep to over the last two years. He usually felt pretty comfortable being gay, but this morning, with the rain beating down, it seemed equally possible that he might be transgender, with just enough time left to straighten himself out before senior year of high school.

Walking to a closet in his bedroom — some of it is a story: a closet door, a nightgown slipping over the bedpost, a nightgown slipping to the floor — he opened the door, stepped inside, and reached for the clothes hanger on the second rack. His jeans hung behind a blue dress and two blouses, and his T-shirts and sweatshirts, between those and the shorts, that he would check when his mother wasn't around anymore.

When I was a kid, apple pie was my favorite. Nothing like it coming out of the oven. The brown sugars turned golden. The crust grew golden too, the sides bubbling and the tops reaching out over the crimped edges. I'd cut a wedge and then run my knife between the apples and the crust. The filling would ooze out almost unbidden, glossy with cinnamon, and then be pulled apart by the knife. I'd lick the shiny juice off the blade before cutting myself another piece. The first thing I look for in an apple pie is the length of the stem. The stems of the apples on the pie should be placed toward the center of each fruit, the stems pointing in the right direction. This does not happen by itself. It takes great care. My second criteria is the apples themselves. Don't even talk to me if you are using commercial pie apples that hold their shape, even under severe heat. Apple slices have a natural tendency to fall apart in well-made pastry. They're not pieces of beef, and cutting them into one- and two-inch pieces should suggest the sweetness of the apple. They're the real thing. The third criteria is the baking oven. It's not the way he or she makes the pastry. It's not whether or not the apples have been blanched before mixing. It's not whether or not they're mixed in with oats or breadcrumbs or nuts or sugar (they're not). It's not whether or not they're sprinkled with cinnamon before baking. A good apple pie must be baked in a good baking oven that is not too hot. This is the most difficult aspect of pie baking. When he finished the fair, Tyler was going to drive to California to visit his grandmother. She remembered when he was born, but the rest of his childhood was blank in her mind as though it had been wiped completely clean.

After Tyler left the fair, he took a detour into the woods along the river where he and his father used to camp when Tyler was little. He had more than $143 in his pocket, which was strange because his father had always told him that money wasn't worth the paper it was printed on. On days like this, he missed his dad so much that he could hardly stand it. He thought about the joy and surprise in his dad's face when Tyler won. He had won for his dad, to prove to him that Tyler could do anything he set his mind to. He had won for his grandmother, too, to show her that it wasn't too late for Tyler to take care of her.

As Tyler walked, he noticed a fallen tree with its roots exposed, and sitting amidst the roots was a shiny coin—a larger than average penny. It was dated 1915, making it more than a century old. He thought of his father's old stories about finding "lucky pennies" and how they held magical powers. Picking it up, he felt a strange sense of connection and lightened mood.

When Tyler arrived home, he placed the penny next to his blue ribbon, feeling a deep sense of achievement and a lighter heart, as though a piece of his father was right there with him. To write an engaging story continuation, let's focus on how Tyler's life evolves in the coming weeks and months post-fair, specifically linking back to his win at the Delmar County Fair and the discovery of the old penny.

After the initial media buzz faded, Tyler found a new confidence in himself, bolstered by his parents and, particularly, his grandmother. She, under the watchful eye of her home healthcare aide, gushed over the ribbon and the details of his win, now a cherished memory for her, too.

The $143 from his win was invested in a college savings account, but he decided to spend the bulk of the additional winnings from his generous parents on his own. Evelyn drove home the long distance on auto-pilot. No one tried to make conversation. She had lost. She had never lost before. Evelyn's mind kept going back to the white box, and she kept seeing Tyler's face in the tent.

That evening Tyler was excited and nervous, as if he were going on stage. His family was there along with most of his friends and other pie entrants, congratulating him. His mom was crying. His step-dad-to-be smiled at his mom, then at Tyler, and raised his glass in a toast: "To Tyler's first place pie. I can't wait to get a slice."

Evelyn played the evening over in her head after she got home. She had been a fool to slip up with the box. Much worse, she might have stolen her victory, which was now Tyler's, all in one small, irresistible moment. Of everything she would have to live with, that was the thing that would eat away at her. She could not sleep and stared into the darkness for a long time, thinking.

Two days later, Evelyn took the grand prize award ribbon off Tyler's pie and replaced it with a smaller, blue ribbon. The cooks who had come to eat the prize-winning pie were disappointed, but they could understand a mistake had been made. Noticing the change in her pie chart that morning, Tyler felt confused and disappointed, but again said nothing.

The next night, Tyler's aunt Jean called and told him that the chief of police would like to talk to him about being a victim of a crime. She wanted to know if he had any suspicions.

Tyler knew exactly what had happened. He took the pie off the prize table and drove home to the smell of fresh apples coming out of the pie pan in his oven. He had been waiting over a week for the exact moment when he would have his blue ribbon and $150. He picked up his phone and called the detective: "I should have seen it coming. I guess you could call that justice."

Tyler Nguyen! Tyler?"

Tyler stepped forward. "Thank you, thank you, Judge Lund, thank you so much." He could see a familiar shape behind the judge and noticed the judge wobble the ribbon. Tyler held out his hand, but Margaret pulled back. "Sir, I think you may not be aware that your entry cannot be your own..."

"Margaret!" a voice called from the crowd. Tyler turned, and his sister Mia waved him over to their mother, standing on her tiptoes so tall. Tyler poked his yellow name tag through the opening in the ribbon and masked his surprise with a smile.

"Mama! Este lienzo a quin?" he asked.

"Your father sent it for you." Her mascara had run, and she fanned her face. "It's spelled r-i-e-n-t-a-r, but your father..."

"Your father has made a large contribution to the fair this year, so this ribbon is for his donation," Margaret told the crowd.

A man near the front called, "Isn't that corrupt?"

"Do you doubt my word?" Margaret demanded. "Did you not see Evelyn's shrink-wrapped pie at the registration table?"

Tyler didn't see his father push through the crowd. He was surprised to see a leather belt and TWO pistols, buttoned in place. People backed away from him, judging by their voices. Tyler was confused, then embarrassed, until his mother grabbed his shoulder. "They already have a long-running controversy with our parish," she said.

His father's voice was low but carried through the tent despite its loudness. "I rented it." He showed the judge the lease.

"Rented what?" the man in the crowd asked.

Tyler sighed. "Pistols," he said. "To show it's rented, his name's on it." The other kids in the crowd froze. "R-i-e-n-t-a-r," he demonstrated.

Then he turned back to the crowd. "I baked it myself. It's not about the ribbon or the money," he said. "It's about victory. Y como que me esmero." The old hands at Thursday night's church service had told Tyler that if he had ever been in trouble, his father would take care of it. Tyler did not believe it, until now.

To his surprise, Tyler saw a puzzled facia on Evelyn's face and turned to see her holding out the blue ribbon. "Keep your prize, Tyler," she said. Then she walked out.
